tracking+pipeline.summary:
I built the tracking area: models.py, tracking.py, segmentation.py and pipeline.py, plus their tests (81 passed with the real models). Main decisions:

- **models.py**: two pinned models (`face_landmarker`, `selfie_multiclass`). A file already on disk with the right SHA-256 is used without touching the network. Otherwise it downloads to a temporary `.part` file in the same folder, checks the SHA-256, then renames it into place (`os.replace`). The partial file is always removed, and a bad download leaves any earlier file untouched. Errors are Japanese and say what to do: offline (with the URL and folder for a manual download), HTTP status, SSL certificate (macOS "Install Certificates.command" hint), wrong hash, and disk full or no write permission.
- **tracking.py**: a vectorised One Euro filter (each point gets its own cutoff). The speed term is measured in eye-corner distances per second, so one slider value feels the same near and far. Slider mapping, documented in `smoothing_params()`: 0 = raw landmarks; above 0, `min_cutoff` falls geometrically from 6 Hz to 0.3 Hz and `beta` from 20 to 4. At 0.5 that is 1.3 Hz / 8.9. I tuned it on synthetic head motion: at 0.5, resting jitter roughly halves and lag during a fast head sway (about 500 px/s) stays around 1 px. **Detection change from the contract:** feeding the whole 16:9 frame (downscaled to 640) missed the face in frame_dark and frame_far. So the tracker feeds a square window (side = frame height, downscaled to 640) that slowly pans after the face, at most 2% of the window per frame. Bigger jumps made MediaPipe drop the face. With no face it tries centre, left, then right. In tests this found every face, including on a moving dim sequence where the full frame missed 22 of 150 frames, and cut landmark jitter about 4x (0.39 to 0.09 px). The detector threshold is 0.3 (MediaPipe default 0.5); the face-presence check stays at 0.5, and there were no false faces on 6 non-face images, including a cat. Also: timestamps sent to MediaPipe always increase, the filter resets when the face is lost or the frame size changes, and models are loaded from bytes because MediaPipe can't open non-ASCII paths on Windows (for example a Japanese user name).
- **segmentation.py**: model input downscaled to a long side of 384, run every N frames, temporal average with alpha 0.5 per run, then upsampled to full frame. Masks are read-only arrays; skipped frames get the same arrays back. **By default it runs on a background thread** — MediaPipe releases Python's lock while it runs (I measured this), so the camera loop never waits about 100 ms for it. Frame-size changes, `reset()`, and a pause of more than 500 ms between calls drop the old masks and any result still in flight. An error from a background run is raised once, at the next `update()` call.
- **pipeline.py**: as in the contract. Notable behaviour:
  - Thread safety: settings are copied under a lock; a separate lock stops `close()` from freeing the models while a frame is processing.
  - Errors: tracker, segmenter and each effect are isolated, and each error is logged once per source and message.
  - Fade: 6 frames in and 6 out, done by scaling `ctx.intensity` of face effects instead of blending whole frames. Fade-out reuses the last landmarks, but never ones older than 500 ms.
  - Segmentation runs only when a hair effect or the skin effect will actually run.
  - Conversion: uint8 to float32 once per frame, clip, `convertScaleAbs` back. No conversion happens when nothing runs.
  - Previews: mirrored per setting; landmark dots go on the preview only.
  - Timings and loading: timings recorded per stage; built-in effects load lazily only when `effects=None`; `process()` after `close()` passes frames through.
- **Visual check:** in the masks render, hair, face-skin and body-skin align on all five test images. In the landmark preview (mirrored crops), points sit correctly on frame_720p, dark, tilt and far.

tracking+pipeline.open_issues:
- **Smoothing tuning:** only tuned on synthetic noise (0.7 px) and synthetic motion; check the slider default with a real webcam.
- **Window panning:** very fast sideways head moves (faster than 2% of the window per frame) can lose the face for a few frames; it is re-found by the retry and search.
- **Small or dim faces:** the 0.3 detector threshold is what lets frame_far be detected (at 0.4 it is missed); faces even smaller than frame_far's are not handled.
- **Failing effects:** an effect that edits the frame in place and then raises leaves its partial change in the frame. I chose not to copy the frame before every effect, for speed.
- **Fade depends on effects:** it assumes each effect scales its strength with `ctx.intensity` and is an exact no-op at 0, as the contract requires.
- **Segmentation speed:** about 100 ms per model run in this container. With the background thread that no longer blocks frames; it only delays the masks.
- **Other agents' files:** conftest.py and tests/data were created by another agent. My real-model tests use its `models_dir` and `face_frame_720p` fixtures. tests/data/face_landmarks_720p.npy may differ by about 1 px from what the new window-based tracker produces.
tracking+pipeline.perf:
Measured in this 4-core container on $SCRATCH/testimgs/frame_720p.png (1280x720, noisy frames, 30 fps pacing):
- **Landmarks**, `FaceTracker.detect` (window 720 scaled to 640 + MediaPipe + filter): median 11.6 ms, p90 14.8 ms per frame. Inside the pipeline, while segmentation runs in the background: median 12.8 ms, p90 14.3 ms.
- **Segmentation, one model run done inline** (input 384x216, plus the temporal average and upsampling three masks to 720p): median 102–107 ms, p90 104–126 ms. Input size barely matters: 256 and 384 both take about 100 ms.
- **Segmentation as the pipeline uses it** (background thread): cost on the processing thread is median 0.0 ms, p90 about 6 ms (the frames where a finished result is merged and upsampled); the first masks are ready after about 4–7 frames.
- **Pipeline with no-op hair and lips effects**, interval 2: total median 17.9 ms, p90 25.8 ms per frame (landmarks + float conversion about 0.9 ms + back to uint8 about 1 ms + mirroring).
- **Full frame vs window, earlier probe:** detecting on the whole frame at 1280 / 640 cost 10.5 / 9.8 ms, so the window costs about the same.

geometry+blend.summary:
Built the geometry layer: makeup_cam/regions.py, makeup_cam/blend.py, shared test fixtures and a landmark fixture made with the real model.

**Landmark indices** (MediaPipe 478-point topology). I picked them from zoomed index maps of the real model output, then drew them on frame_720p, frame_tilt and frame_far and checked the images.
- Subject-left is on the image right.
- Eye, brow, crease and under-eye lines run from the inner corner to the outer corner.
- The new indices include crease lines, under-eye top and bottom lines, cheek-apple sets, nose-wing outlines, the nose bridge, lip centre points, mouth corners and eye corners.
- `SideIndices` and `side_indices(side)` let effects loop over both sides.
- Tests check the index sets on the committed landmarks: left/right, inner-to-outer order, vertical order, mirror symmetry (under 6% of the eye distance) and nesting.

**Rasterization.** cv2 LINE_AA fills sit about 0.7 px outside the true edge, and a zero-area polygon still comes out as a ~2 px line. So shapes are drawn on a 4x4 supersampled canvas without anti-aliasing and box-filtered down. cv2 fills half a sub-pixel too wide; that is corrected by insetting polygons and shrinking stroke and ellipse radii.
- Edge-on-pixel coverage is exact; areas are within 1-2%.
- A closed-mouth opening vanishes completely.
- Work is limited to the shape's bounding box plus 4 sigma, so a small shape drawn into a whole-face ROI stays cheap.
- Large feathers are rasterized and blurred at reduced resolution; the result stays within about 3% of an exact Gaussian blur.

**Region masks.**
- `lips_mask`: soft outer edge, crisp cut at the mouth opening. `outline` is a fraction of the combined lip thickness.
- `eyelid_mask`: lash line and lower brow edge are resampled by arc length; `height` 0..1 moves the top edge from the lashes to the brow; the eye opening is cut out crisply so the lash line keeps full strength.
- `under_eye_mask`: from the line below the lashes toward the cheekbone, scaled by `depth`, eye excluded.
- `brow_mask`: `thickness` scales the brow height around its centre line.
- `eye_opening_mask` and `face_oval_mask` take `expand_px`.
- `face_scale` is the distance between the two eye-corner midpoints. When the head turns, an eyes-to-nose-base measure takes over so sizes stay steady.

**blend.py.** Implements the contract functions with in-place maths and dtype kept. `mix` and `apply_color` return the input unchanged, bit for bit, when the mask or opacity is 0; at opacity 0 `apply_color` returns the input array itself.
- Soft light uses the Pegtop formula.
- "color" mode keeps Lab L, takes the colour's a/b and uses float32 cvtColor. Where that chroma cannot be displayed at a pixel's lightness, it is cut back to the most the sRGB range allows, so blacks and whites stay neutral. That limit is computed once per colour, cached, and applied with cv2.LUT.
- Rendered lipstick in each mode (`blend_modes_lips.png`); "color" looks natural and the teeth are untouched.

**Fixtures.** tests/conftest.py provides `face_frame_720p` (built exactly as specified), `face_landmarks_720p`, `models_dir` and `fake_ctx`, which returns `make_ctx(...)`.
- tests/data/face_landmarks_720p.npy (3.9 KB) comes from tests/data/generate_face_landmarks.py: VIDEO mode, 15 frames until the points stop moving.
- I generated it three times: maximum difference 0.0 px. A test in test_regions.py runs the script again and compares (skipped without models).

These are deviations from the contract or additions to it.

**Iris indices.** The contract says `LEFT_IRIS` is in the 468-472 range, but on the real model 468-472 is the subject's RIGHT iris. Following the subject-left convention:
- `LEFT_IRIS = [474, 475, 476, 477]` (closed ring), `LEFT_IRIS_CENTER = 473`
- `RIGHT_IRIS = [469, 470, 471, 472]`, `RIGHT_IRIS_CENTER = 468`

**Index constants are plain lists.** `landmarks[LIPS_OUTER]` works and `+` concatenates. Do not mutate them.

**New regions.py names:**
- `Side`, `SIDES`, `SideIndices`, `side_indices(side)` (raises ValueError for a bad side)
- `eye_center(lm, side)`, `cheek_center(lm, side)`, `resample_polyline(points, n)`
- `LIPS_UPPER_OUTER`, `LIPS_LOWER_OUTER`, `LIPS_UPPER_INNER`, `LIPS_LOWER_INNER` (open lines, subject-right corner to subject-left corner)
- `LIPS_TOP` = 0, `LIPS_INNER_TOP` = 13, `LIPS_INNER_BOTTOM` = 14, `LIPS_BOTTOM` = 17
- `MOUTH_RIGHT_CORNER` = 61, `MOUTH_LEFT_CORNER` = 291
- `{LEFT,RIGHT}_EYE_{INNER,OUTER}_CORNER`
- `{LEFT,RIGHT}_EYE_CREASE`, `{LEFT,RIGHT}_UNDER_EYE_{TOP,BOTTOM}`, `{LEFT,RIGHT}_BROW_{UPPER,LOWER}` (index-wise pairs), `{LEFT,RIGHT}_NOSE_WING` (closed outlines)
- `NOSE_BOTTOM` = 2, `NOSE_BRIDGE`
- `NOSE_TIP` = 1, the MediaPipe nose-tip point. In this portrait it shows slightly below the bright spot on the tip; point 4 is just above it.

**regions.py signatures:**
- `roi_around(points, shape, pad=0.25, margin_px=0.0)`: `pad` is a fraction of the bounding box's larger side; use `margin_px` of about 3x the feather.
- `polyline_mask(points, thickness_px, roi, feather_px=0.0, thickness_profile=None)`: `thickness_px` is the full width; round joins and caps.
- `ellipse_mask(center_xy, axes_xy, angle_deg, roi, feather_px=0.0)`: `axes_xy` are semi-axes; angle follows the cv2 convention.
- `lips_mask(lm, roi, outline=0.0, feather_px=0.0)`: `outline` is a fraction of the combined lip thickness; settings range ±0.2 is about ±7% of the eye distance.
- `eye_opening_mask(lm, side, roi, expand_px=0.0, feather_px=0.0)`
- `brow_mask(lm, side, roi, thickness=0.0, feather_px=0.0)`: thickness is relative (+0.5 = 1.5x).
- `face_oval_mask(lm, roi, expand_px=0.0, feather_px=0.0)`
- `under_eye_mask(lm, side, roi, depth=1.0, feather_px=0.0)` and `eyelid_mask(lm, side, roi, height, feather_px=0.0)`: both exclude the eye opening and return zeros at depth or height 0.
- All feather defaults are 0. Effects should pass k * face_scale.

**face_scale** returns max(eye distance, eyes-to-nose-base / 0.8). For frontal faces this equals the eye distance.

**blend.py:**
- Public `blend_color(base, color)`; type aliases `Color` and `BlendMode`.
- `apply_color(base, color, mask, opacity, mode)`: `mask=None` means the whole image; opacity is clamped to 0..1; opacity 0 returns `base` itself; an unknown mode raises ValueError.
- "color" mode reduces chroma to what can be displayed at each pixel's lightness instead of clipping. Colours that can be displayed get the colour's exact a/b; black and white stay neutral.
- `soft_light` uses the Pegtop formula.
- `adjust_brightness_contrast`: brightness is an additive offset; contrast is relative around `pivot`, which defaults to the mask-weighted mean luminance. With both at 0 it returns the input.
- `luminance` uses 0.299R + 0.587G + 0.114B.

**conftest:**
- Fixture `fake_ctx` returns `make_ctx(frame, landmarks, hair_mask=None, face_skin_mask=None, intensity=1.0, body_skin_mask=None)`.
- Also exports `build_face_frame_720p()`, `FACE_LANDMARKS_720P` and `DATA_DIR`.
geometry+blend.open_issues:
1. **Finding for the tracking agent.** On a 1280x720 frame, the first Face Landmarker result is vertically wrong by up to about 28 px (IMAGE mode, or the first VIDEO frame); the mesh comes out stretched. Tracking the same image in VIDEO mode settles in about 10 frames: under 0.25 px change by frame 6, 0.03 px by frame 12. Separately, the full-frame detector misses the small face (frame_far) and the dim face (frame_dark), but finds both on a square centre crop. Suggestion: run the initial detection on a square crop or padded frame, or simply expect a few unsteady frames after the face is first found.
2. MediaPipe's upper brow row sits above thin brow hair, so `brow_mask` also covers some skin above the brow. The brow effect should weight by pixel darkness or use negative thickness.
3. Accuracy limits: feathered masks are within about 3% of an exact Gaussian, and slivers thinner than 1/4 px (coarser under large feathers) vanish. This is intended, but effects should not rely on sub-quarter-pixel polygons.
4. Blending over a whole close-up face ROI (346x394) costs several ms on this container: about 5 ms for "color" mode and 3 ms for soft light. The skin and hair effects should restrict to tight ROIs or downscale. Lip-sized ROIs take 0.2-0.5 ms.
5. Timings come from a shared, slow 4-core container while other agents were running, taking the best of 5 runs.
6. pytest creates __pycache__ and .pytest_cache under ROOT. The integrator should add a .gitignore.

camera+runner.summary:
Built makeup_cam/camera.py and makeup_cam/runner.py, with their tests.

camera.py:
- **Capture backends:** DirectShow then Media Foundation on Windows, AVFoundation on macOS, V4L2 on Linux. The MJPG format is set before width/height (DirectShow and V4L2 only); then size, then fps.
- **Open check:** `open()` reads up to 5 frames to confirm the camera works. If a backend opens but gives no frames, it falls back to the next one. Failure raises the new `CameraError` with a Japanese, per-OS fix (Windows camera privacy toggle / other apps using the camera, macOS camera permission for the terminal, Linux /dev/video permissions).
- **Reading:** `read()` never raises and converts gray or 4-channel frames to BGR. After 15 failed reads in a row it releases the device and reopens it, at most once every 2 s.
- **`list_cameras`:**
  - Opens each index once and reads no frames.
  - OpenCV's warnings are silenced only while probing, and the old log level is restored after.
  - Without names, it probes indices in order and stops after 2 misses in a row past index 0. It also stops starting new probes after 6 s.
  - Linux: names come from /sys/class/video4linux, only known devices are probed, and virtual cameras (OBS Virtual Camera, v4l2loopback, our own "AI Makeup Cam") are skipped.
  - Windows/macOS: names are "カメラ N".
  - New keyword `in_use=`: indices the app already has open are listed without probing them again.
- **`VirtualCameraOutput`:** imports pyvirtualcam only when created, opens it in BGR with fps printing off, and does not use its built-in frame pacing. A frame of a different size is scaled to fit and centered on black, so its shape is never distorted. Every failure becomes a `VirtualCameraError` with the Japanese steps from the contract per OS, plus the original error text.

runner.py uses two background threads per `start()`:
- **Capture thread:** owns the camera. It retries opening every `retry_interval_s` (2 s), recreates a camera object that raises, and keeps only the newest frame. Slow camera opens on Windows block only this thread.
- **Output thread:** owns the virtual camera. It runs the pipeline on the newest frame and drops old ones, so delay never builds up. It sends results to the virtual camera and `on_frame`.
  - If no frame arrives for `camera_timeout_s` (1 s), it sends a cached dark "camera off" frame with the text "Camera reconnecting..." at the target fps. That frame also goes to the GUI preview.
  - If `pipeline.process` raises, the raw frame is sent instead and `processing_error` is set.
  - If the virtual camera fails to open or send, it is closed and retried every 2 s while video processing continues.
- **Status:** FPS and processing time are smoothed averages and reset to 0 while the camera is lost. `on_status` fires on any state change and at least every 0.5 s. A last all-default status is sent when the runner stops.
- **Commands:** `set_camera` and `set_virtual_camera` only update locked fields, and the thread that owns the device applies them. `set_camera` always reconnects; a new size also reopens the virtual camera at that size. Settings and bypass go straight to the thread-safe pipeline.
- **Start/stop:** both can be called repeatedly and the runner can be restarted. `stop()` joins the threads within its timeout, works when called from a callback, and does not close the pipeline. Errors are logged once each: known camera and virtual camera errors without a traceback, others with one.

The read-only check of the concurrently written gui.py shows it already calls `list_cameras(in_use=...)` and the runner API as built here.

Additions to the contract; all contract names are unchanged:
- camera.py:
  - New `CameraError(RuntimeError)`, raised by `CameraSource.open()` with a Japanese message.
  - `CameraInfo` is frozen; width/height are the driver's default size, 0 when unknown.
  - `list_cameras(max_index=8, *, in_use=(), time_budget_s=6.0, capture_factory=cv2.VideoCapture)`: pass `in_use={runner.camera_index}` so the open camera is listed without being probed again.

  - `VirtualCameraOutput` has `.width`, `.height`, `.fps` and `.device` (str). `send()` raises `VirtualCameraError`, also after `close()`. It scales mismatched frames to fit and pads with black instead of stretching them.
  - Public helpers: `fit_frame`, `host_os()` ("windows", "macos", "linux" or "other"), `capture_backends()`, `quiet_opencv_logs`, `camera_open_error_message`, `virtual_camera_error_message`, `VIRTUAL_CAMERA_LABEL="AI Makeup Cam"`.
  - Importing camera.py sets the environment variable OPENCV_VIDEOIO_MSMF_ENABLE_HW_TRANSFORMS=0 if it is not already set (avoids 10+ s Media Foundation opens).
- runner.py:
  - `RunnerStatus` is frozen, all fields have defaults, and there is one extra field `processing_error: str | None`.
  - `CameraRunner` has extra keywords `retry_interval_s=2.0` and `camera_timeout_s=1.0`, and extra read-only properties `camera_index` and `is_running`.
  - Factories are called with keyword arguments: `camera_factory(index=, width=, height=, fps=)` and `vcam_factory(width=, height=, fps=)`.
  - `set_camera` always reconnects, even with the same index; a changed size also reopens the virtual camera at that size.
  - `on_frame` also receives placeholder results while the camera is lost (output, preview and original_preview are the placeholder; face_found is False).
  - `on_status` fires on state changes, at least every 0.5 s, and once more with `RunnerStatus()` when the runner stops.
  - `stop()` does not close the pipeline.
  - Public `placeholder_frame(w, h)` (cached, read-only) plus the message constants CAMERA_LOST_MESSAGE, CAMERA_READ_FAILED_MESSAGE and PROCESSING_FAILED_MESSAGE.
camera+runner.open_issues:
- **No real devices tested:** none exist in this container. The DirectShow/MSMF fallback, the MJPG hint, the macOS permission flow and the pyvirtualcam OBS backends were checked only with fakes, plus one Linux run with no devices.
- **Windows/macOS camera names:** these are "カメラ N" because there is no cheap way to get real names. So OBS Virtual Camera cannot be filtered out there, and a user could pick it as input and create a feedback loop.
- **Index shift:** if a webcam is unplugged and indices shift, reconnecting index N may open a different device.
- **Hung pipeline:** a `pipeline.process()` that hangs rather than raises freezes the virtual camera output. There is deliberately no separate sending thread.
- **Stop timeout:** a thread still blocked in a driver call when the stop timeout ends is left running as a background thread, with a warning logged. It closes its device when the call returns.

effect:skin.summary:
Built `SkinEffect` ("skin", order 20) in makeup_cam/effects/skin.py, a natural skin retouch that works only inside the face-oval ROI. Results at a glance: the default look is subtle and natural, it runs in about 3.5–3.7 ms on the 720p fixture, and 53 tests pass.

How it works:
- **One working grid.** All analysis runs on a downscaled copy of the ROI where the face scale is about 40 px, whatever the distance to the camera. Every step is folded into one per-channel affine model, `out = patch*(1-shade) + lift`. That model is upsampled and applied to the full-resolution patch in about 5 array operations. Full-res edges and texture survive, and pixels outside the masks come back bit for bit.
- **Masks.** The skin area is the face oval (shrunk 0.07×scale, feathered 0.1×scale) times the segmentation face-skin mask. If there is no face-skin mask, `1 - hair_mask` is used. A face-skin mask covering under 35% of the oval is ignored. Two feature masks are built:
  - **Wide (smoothing, blemish):** eyes, brows grown 1.8×, mouth, and nostril ellipses fitted with `minAreaRect`. Each shape is fully protected up to its outline and fades outward.
  - **Tight (colour edits):** no brows. Colour edits also skip pixels darker than 0.35–0.7× the face's median L, so brow hairs, lashes and nostril shadows are left alone while the skin between brow hairs is still covered. This removed the light rings and brow bands that showed at extreme dark shades.
- **Smoothing.** A fast guided filter (He & Sun) computed on the working grid. The `texture` slider keeps a share of the fine detail (patch minus a blurred copy), folded into the same model, so it costs nothing extra at full resolution.
- **Blemish cover.** The first version used the suggested median-difference test, and the renders showed it erasing smile lines and creases. It was replaced by a scale-normalized Hessian blob detector on the green channel, with a scale test `r(σ) − max(r(2σ), 0)`. This responds only to compact spots, not to lines or larger shading such as the nose-wing crease. Spots are filled with the average of the surrounding skin, leaving the spots themselves out. On a synthetic test, a spot loses 61% of its darkness while a line of the same contrast is untouched.
- **Colour (Lab, on the working grid).**
  - **Redness:** a* above the face's median + 1.5 is reduced.
  - **Concealer:** fills the under-eye darkness toward the median L and cancels the bluish cast, with a lash guard that is solid inside the eye.
  - **Foundation:** evens chroma toward `tone_color`, but the face's average only moves 60% of the way. This stops the face from parting from the neck in warm light.
  - **Brightness:** changes L by a share of the headroom, so highlights never clip.
- **Exact no-op** when all sliders are 0, `ctx.intensity` is 0, there are no landmarks, the face scale is under 10 px, or the face is mostly outside the frame. Input landmarks and masks are never written; the frame ROI is edited in place.

Visual tuning used the real `MakeupPipeline` with only this effect (synchronous segmenter) on frame_720p, frame_dark, frame_tilt, frame_far and a webcam-scale close-up (face scale about 130 px) cut from the astronaut image, across many slider settings. Defaults read as natural makeup: freckles and blotches reduced, under-eyes a little brighter, nose and smile-line shading kept. Strong settings are airbrushed but have no hard edges, halos or changes on teeth, eyes or background.

The only default I changed is `SkinSettings.blemish`, 0.3 → 0.5, because the new detector is conservative.

effect:lips_blush.summary:
Built LipEffect ("lips", order 70) and BlushEffect ("blush", order 60). Both run through the real MakeupPipeline, and I tuned them visually over several rounds on frame_720p, frame_dark, frame_tilt, frame_far and a synthetic close-up (frame_720p upscaled 2x). I kept the config defaults as they were; they already gave a natural interview look.

LIPS (makeup_cam/effects/lips.py):
- Mask: regions.lips_mask. The feather (scale*(0.006+0.035*feather)) applies to the outer lip line only; the edge toward the teeth stays crisp, so teeth are never touched (a test checks they are bit-identical).
- Color: blend.blend_color (lipstick hue and chroma, lip shading kept), plus the lips' average Lab L moves 70% toward the lipstick's L, so nudes lighten and berries darken. Mixed by paint*opacity*intensity.
- Added beyond the guidance (scene-cast adaptation): the first renders showed that "color" mode uses absolute a/b, so a nude under the warm frame_dark light came out lavender. Now the lipstick a/b is shifted by 0.75 x (median a/b of the brighter half of the skin ring around the mouth minus a typical skin chroma (11, 18)). The shift is capped at 20 Lab units and rounded to 0.5 so it stays steady and the gamut cache stays hot.
- Finish: matte compresses lightness above the lips' median before recoloring. An earlier version flattened after recoloring and left a gray blob, and a highlight-map version left ring artifacts. Satin and gloss find highlights on the lips' luminance smoothed over the lips only (normalized convolution, 80th to 99th percentile ramp, smoothstep), then screen the scene light level (99th percentile luminance, clipped to 0.3..1) onto them. Gloss also spreads the shine and adds a soft oval reflection on the lower lip.
- Strength rules: matte is part of the pigment, so it scales with opacity. Shine reaches full strength from opacity 0.3, because a sheer gloss still shines. Opacity 0 or intensity 0 returns the frame unchanged.
- Close-up faces (face scale > 90 px) are processed on a downscaled ROI. The upsampled change is added back and masked by the full-resolution mouth opening.

BLUSH (makeup_cam/effects/blush.py):
- One ellipse per cheek in a face-aligned frame: across is the eye line, down is perpendicular to it, and outward is mirrored per side. So the blush follows head roll, offset_x moves both outward, and offset_y moves down.
- The center is regions.cheek_center plus the shape's own shift plus the sliders.
- Head yaw: the horizontal axis on each side is squeezed by (apple-to-contour distance at landmarks 234/93 or 454/323) / (0.44*scale), clipped to 0.3..1.25.
- Shapes: round = circle; oval = wide, lifted 10 degrees; lifted = narrow, 28 degrees, shifted outward and up. The image-space ellipse comes from an SVD of the linear map.
- Masks are rendered on a coarse grid (face scale about 24 px) using the regions helpers with transformed coordinates, then upsampled.
- Allowed area: face oval shrunk by max(0.06*scale, 1.5 sigma), times the face_skin_mask when present (ignored if it covers less than 35% of the blush). Keep-out zones: the eyes and lips grow with the guard softness (at least 2.5 sigma) so they stay clean even at softness 1. A convex hull of nose plus lips removes the "mustache" band under the nose that showed up in an early render.
- Blend: I compared soft-light, multiply, color, tint and mixes, and chose 60% multiply + 40% soft light. It reads as a flush in the skin and picks up the scene light. It is computed in closed form with cv2.transform/multiply/add for speed; a test checks it matches blend.mix of blend_soft_light and blend_multiply to 1e-6.

Both effects work inside an ROI, write in place, return float32 in [0,1], and leave everything outside the ROI bit-identical.

effect:eyes_brows.summary:
I built the eyeshadow, eyeliner and brow effects and tuned them by rendering through the real MakeupPipeline. At default settings all three look natural: the eyes look a little more defined and the brows a little fuller, with no visible filter look. All 110 tests pass, and every effect stays under the 4 ms target at 1280x720 (about 1.2–1.5 ms each in direct runs on the test frame, up to 2.9 ms on a 2x close-up).

EyeshadowEffect ("eyeshadow", order 40):
- Where it goes: the lid between the upper lash line and the lower edge of the brow. The eye opening is always cut out with a crisp edge, so the eyeball is never tinted. When the eye closes, the shadow covers the closed lid.
- How it fades: each pixel gets a lid position (0 at the lash line, 1 at the chosen height), computed from its distances to the lash line and to the brow. The shadow follows the lash line near the eye and fans out toward the brow tail higher up. It is densest at the lash line, fades upward (softness widens the fade), and is deeper toward the outer corner. Past the outer corner it fades out softly above a line rising 12° from the corner, so the corner lifts instead of drooping.
- Why I changed the approach: feathering the shared `regions.eyelid_mask` shrank it to a thin crescent, left a faint line along the lower lid, and made a hard triangle at full height. Those problems are why I switched to the distance-based fade.
- Color: a mix of multiply and soft light, so the lid keeps its texture and the shadow takes on the room's lighting.
- Shimmer: a soft sheen on the centre of the lid, scaled by the room's brightness and by how lit each pixel already is. It is tied to the landmarks, so it does not flicker between frames.

EyelinerEffect ("eyeliner", order 50):
- A line along the upper lash line, hairline-thin at the inner corner and full width toward the outer corner. It sits just above the lash line and is cut by the eye opening.
- The wing rises at 20° from the outer corner and tapers to a point; its length grows with the wing slider, relative to face size.
- The optional lower line covers the outer two thirds of the lower lid, thinner and softer than the upper line.
- The pigment never lightens dark lashes. A minimum blur keeps thin lines continuous on small faces instead of dashed.
- In a simulated blink the liner follows the closing lid.

BrowEffect ("brows", order 30):
- The brow outline is a smooth curve through the brow landmarks, made thicker or thinner by the thickness slider, with a pointed tail.
- The fill is weighted by how dense the real hairs are, compared against the surrounding skin (dark bangs, lashes and shadows are excluded). Colour goes onto and between the real hairs, with a light floor so sparse tails still get filled. If the landmarks drift (for example while raising the eyebrows), the colour stays on the real brow instead of drawing a second brow beside it.
- An earlier version deliberately coloured hairs less than the skin between them. At strong settings that made the original hairs lighter than the filled skin around them. I removed it: plain multiply darkens skin much more than already-dark hairs, so hairs always stay darker and the texture survives even at full strength with a near-black colour.

Every effect leaves the frame unchanged when its opacity or the master intensity is 0, or when no face is found. All work happens in a small area around each eye or brow, with sizes scaled to face size. None of the effects need the hair or skin masks.

Defaults: I raised the eyeshadow opacity default from 0.28 to 0.5, because at 0.28 the change was about 8 brightness levels out of 255, too faint to see even side by side. The eyeliner and brow defaults are unchanged.

- Brows: if bangs cover the brow, the dark hair can count as brow hair and pull some fill onto it. Multiply on dark hair changes little in absolute terms, but nothing excludes hair yet; I deliberately did not use hair_mask, because the segmentation model may label the brows themselves as hair.
- Eyeshadow shimmer is a soft sheen only, with no glitter sparkle (the guidance allowed this). It scales with opacity up to 0.3, like lip gloss does, so shimmer alone at opacity 0 does nothing.
- The test portrait has small faces (face size about 58 px, about 33 px when far). I checked typical webcam size with a synthetic 2x close-up only, not real webcam footage.
- At extremes (max thickness, softness 0, near-black colour) the brow is an obviously drawn-on shape. That is intended for extreme settings; it shows no inversion or jagged edges.
- Speed: the three effects together take about 4.9 ms at 720p inside the pipeline (about 7.3 ms on the 2x close-up), roughly a third of the 15 ms total effect budget. I kept the code readable rather than micro-optimizing, since most of the time is fixed per-call overhead on this slow container.

effect:hair.summary:
I built makeup_cam/effects/hair.py: HairEffect, name "hair", order 10, needs_face=False, needs_hair_mask=True. Its 46 tests pass. At default settings the change is very subtle on every test frame (the interviewer-won't-notice level). I tuned it in many rounds with the real MakeupPipeline on the 4 test frames, a close framing, and 4 real dark-haired actors from the CREMA-D clips in scratch. I added the actor frames because the portrait's hair is light. A synthetic dark-hair test I tried first was misleading: the segmenter barely detected it.

**Where the effect applies**
- The hair mask is searched for blobs on a coarse grid. Blobs away from the face are dropped as background false positives; without a face, the largest blobs are kept.
- The ROI is the bounding box of the kept blobs. Blob results are reused while the segmenter returns the same mask array.
- Face skin is subtracted twice: before the confidence threshold, and again after the edge feather.
- The inner face (eyes, nose, mouth, inner cheeks) and both brows are always protected using the landmarks. This also covers the case where the mask lags behind a moving head.
- edge_softness only fades effects inward from the hair edge. Spreading outward left a dark halo on light walls when darkening, so it never does.

**Grids (cost does not depend on distance to the camera)**
- Analysis runs on a working copy at about 36 px per inter-ocular distance (max about 30k pixels).
- The per-pixel look is computed on a render copy at about 48 px per inter-ocular distance (max about 100k pixels).
- Both are integer box downscales, with hysteresis so the resolution does not flicker near a threshold.
- The frame itself only receives `out = in * scale + offset`, so its texture and edges survive.

**まとまり (smoothness)**
- The guidance suggested bilateral filtering. I replaced it with blurring along the strand direction (structure tensor plus four steered line kernels), which combs the hair instead of making it look painted. Where no direction dominates (curls), a small isotropic blur takes over.
- The change is added in the hair's own colour. An earlier gain-based version turned dark gaps red; this fixed it.
- It also trims fine detail a little, and only touches the hair's interior.

**ツヤ (gloss)**
- It boosts the hair's own highlights, measured on hair pixels only. Before that fix, a bright background and the forehead caused rims at the outline and the hairline.
- It adds an "angel ring" arc about 0.25 inter-ocular distances inside the head's silhouette over the top of the head, with a faint sheen even on dark hair.
- The sheen sits on the brighter strands and is partly tinted with the hair's hue, so it looks like shine rather than a grey veil.
- It stays off the outermost strands and is scaled by the scene's light level.

**Hair colour**
- I used per-channel dye gains instead of the suggested Lab colour blend. The hair's mean colour is mapped to the target while each strand keeps its relative light and shade.
- Darkening follows the target fully. Lightening and colour change are limited on hair darker than the target, so red on black hair becomes a dark wine tint.
- The target is adjusted for the scene's colour cast, measured on the forehead skin. Under a warm lamp, dark brown no longer turns ashy or purple.

**Brightness and contrast**
- Contrast is an S-curve around the hair's mean luminance that never clips.
- Brightness is an exposure change that rolls off toward white.
- Colour follows brightening only partly. Before this, lifted shadows turned orange.

Hair statistics are smoothed over frames, and reset() clears them along with the other per-frame state.

effect:hair.api_deviations:
No changes to config.py; the HairSettings fields and defaults are unchanged. No shared module was modified.

- **Colour**: does not call blend.apply_color(mode="color"). It uses per-channel multiplicative dye gains, for the reasons in the summary.
- **Brightness/contrast**: does not call blend.adjust_brightness_contrast. Contrast is a clip-free S-curve pivoting at the hair's mean luminance; brightness is an exposure change, not an additive offset, because an offset washes dark hair to grey.
- **Polygon masks**: the inner-face and brow protection uses a private `_soft_polygons` helper (cv2.fillPoly with anti-aliasing, then a feather) instead of regions.polygon_mask. These masks are heavily feathered, so supersampling only cost time.
- **State**: besides the smoothed statistics, HairEffect keeps the last downscale factors and a blob cache keyed on the mask array; reset() clears all of it. The cache assumes masks are replaced, never edited in place (the segmenter's masks are read-only).
- **Frame handling**: like lips, the effect edits the frame in place inside the ROI and returns it.
- **Test helpers**: tests build FrameContext directly; the conftest fixture is actually named `fake_ctx`, not `make_ctx`.
effect:hair.open_issues:
- **Timing**: on the 720p face frame the effect is slightly over the 4 ms target when all controls are on (about 4.2–4.7 ms); defaults run 3.5–4.0 ms. Close webcam framings (inter-ocular distance 120–130 px) take about 6–7 ms and long hair about 7.5–8.5 ms. Per-frame cost scales with the hair ROI size; the pixel caps bound it but do not reach 4 ms there. Measurements in this container varied by about ±0.4 ms because other agents were running.
- **Dye on blond**: neutral highlights keep their relative difference from the target hue, so vivid colours show slightly pink highlights on blond hair. This looks plausible, but the hue is not exactly the target everywhere.
- **Angel ring**: its position is a geometric guess (fixed depth inside the silhouette, upper head only), toned down where the hair has no real highlight. It could be misplaced for updos, hats or a strong side light.
- **Flyaways**: smoothing only touches the hair's interior, so flyaways sticking out of the silhouette are not removed. That is left for the planned hairstyle work.
- **Bangs**: hair within about 0.2 inter-ocular distances above the brows is treated as face and protected, so very low bangs get weaker effects there.
- **Brittle tuning constants**: the forehead-skin reference used for the colour cast and the ROI size estimate when no face is visible are fixed constants.
- **Test data**: tests use a synthetic hair mask built from the fixture landmarks (about 0.6 IoU with the real mask). Only one test runs the real segmentation model, and it skips without models.
- **Untested**: the gloss strand look was not checked at resolutions above 720p.
